title: Nehemiah 7:1–5
context: With the wall finished and the doors in place, Nehemiah appoints gatekeepers, singers, and Levites, puts Hanani and Hananiah in charge of Jerusalem, and gives orders for guarding the gates. The city is large but thinly populated. God puts it into Nehemiah’s heart to gather the people for registration, and he finds the genealogical record of those who first returned, which the rest of the chapter reproduces.

verses.text: Now when the wall was built and I had set up the doors, and the gatekeepers and the singers and the Levites were appointed,
verses.arminianNotes: The wall is built, the doors set, and gatekeepers, singers, and Levites appointed. Arminian readers note that finishing the wall is not the end of Nehemiah’s work: a city needs faithful people to guard it and worship in it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the order of priorities: once the wall is secure, Nehemiah turns to the people who serve God’s house. Physical protection serves the deeper purpose of restored worship in Jerusalem.

verses.text: I put my brother Hanani, and Hananiah the governor of the fortress, in charge of Jerusalem; for he was a faithful man and feared God above many.
verses.arminianNotes: Nehemiah puts Hanani and Hananiah in charge, noting that Hananiah was faithful and feared God above many. Arminian readers see character, not only competence, as the qualification for leadership.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Hanani is probably the brother who first brought news of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 1:2). Some readers take the two names as referring to one person, though most see two men; the point is the fear of God.

verses.text: I said to them, “Don’t let the gates of Jerusalem be opened until the sun is hot; and while they stand guard, let them shut the doors, and you bar them; and appoint watches of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, everyone in his watch, with everyone near his house.”
verses.arminianNotes: Nehemiah orders the gates kept shut until the sun is hot and sets watches by each house. Arminian readers see prudent vigilance, the practical side of trusting God in a city surrounded by opponents.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that each resident guards near his own house, so that defense becomes everyone’s responsibility. God’s protection does not exclude watchfulness; it works through faithful human watching.

verses.text: Now the city was wide and large; but the people were few therein, and the houses were not built.
verses.arminianNotes: The city is wide and large, but the people are few and the houses not built. Arminian readers see a city with walls but without a community, a reminder that restoration needs people as well as stone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this problem is addressed later when lots are cast to bring one in ten to live in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:1). The emptiness sets up the genealogical record that follows.

verses.text: My God put into my heart to gather together the nobles, and the rulers, and the people, that they might be listed by genealogy. I found the book of the genealogy of those who came up at the first, and I found this written in it:
verses.arminianNotes: My God put into my heart to gather the people. Arminian readers see God prompting a leader who then acts freely and responsibly; the Philippians 2:13 box discusses how the traditions understand God’s work in human desire.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God as the source of Nehemiah’s plan, working inwardly to move him to act. The discovery of the earlier register shows God’s care for the continuity of his people across generations.
